Adversaries could exploit these data to assess vulnerabilities or predict energy consumption patterns of defense-critical infrastructure. Quantum computing advancements anticipated in the next two decades could magnify these cyber vulnerabilities and add uncertainty around legacy cybersecurity best practices, although research on post-quantum cybersecurity protocols is underway (KPMG Global Organization 2025; Torkington 2024). Requiring high procurement cybersecurity standards, testing the cybersecurity of energy assets, and maintaining non-digitized backup generation for critical loads would help mitigate this risk. 4 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2.3 Footprint and Detectability Energy infrastructure has long been a target during conflicts, and adopting advanced energy technology will not shift this paradigm. Although DERs have advantages when it comes to point- of-need generation and resilience, other characteristics can make them more vulnerable to detection and targeting, particularly in contested environments. For example, the larger physical footprint of distributed systems makes them more easily discovered, observed, or identified by adversaries, potentially limiting their applications in sensitive or high-risk areas. Undersea cables bring offshore energy production to consumers and help balance supply and demand across regional power grids. Damage to undersea cables (whether from accidents or intentional interference) is not uncommon and can be repaired in a matter of weeks or months in peacetime (Leadvent Group 2025). An average downtime of 40 days is estimated for intra-array cables and 60 days for export cables (Arikan 2025). Although undersea cables used to transmit electricity are typically located within 50 kilometers from shore (closer than communication cables [McCoy et al. 2024]), they remain vulnerable to sabotage or accidental damage, especially during conflicts, as they are frequently uncrewed and relatively accessible. Especially overseas, DOW might rely on power coming from offshore wind resources reliant on such cables. For example, in Germany, offshore wind energy accounted for 5.9% of the country’s total electricity generation in 2024. With expansion targets set by German law, predictions indicate that offshore wind generation could more than double by 2035 (Deutsche WindGuard 2025). Offshore wind power has expanded off the coasts of the United Kingdom, Germany, Vietnam, and China, and wind plants in the Atlantic serve U.S. power markets. DOW may want to consider obfuscation/camouflage and plan for a certain share of DERs to be inoperable during a conflict. 2.4 Variability of Some Advanced Energy Assets The integration of some advanced energy technologies introduces variability in power generation, requiring energy storage to meet demand during low generation. Although distributed generation increases resilience, it has necessitated more complex planning systems for electric utilities. Photovoltaic (PV) solar generation variability is evident over a 24-hour period, as solar output fluctuates with the time of day and weather conditions (Saxena et al. 2024). Prolonged overcast conditions or unexpected PV system failures can result in periods when backup from the power grid or energy storage assets is needed to meet electricity demand.
